{{good article}}
{{Use British English|date=May 2021}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2026}}
'''Mirkwood''' is any of several great dark [[forest]]s in novels by [[Sir Walter Scott]] and [[William Morris]] in the 19th century, and by [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] in the 20th century. The critic [[Tom Shippey]] explains that the name evoked the excitement of the wildness of Europe's ancient North.<ref name="Shippey2014">{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |title=The Road to Middle-Earth: How J. R. R. Tolkien Created a New Mythology |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qGzAAgAAQBAJ&pg=PT39 |year=2014 |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0-547-52441-2 |page=39}}</ref>

At least two distinct [[Middle-earth]] forests are named Mirkwood in [[Tolkien's legendarium]]. One is in the [[First Age]], when the highlands of Dorthonion north of [[Beleriand]] became known as Mirkwood after falling under [[Morgoth]]'s control. The more famous Mirkwood was in Wilderland, east of the river Anduin. It had acquired the name Mirkwood after it fell under the evil influence of [[Sauron|the Necromancer]] in his fortress of '''Dol Guldur'''<!--redirects here-->; before that it had been known as Greenwood the Great. This Mirkwood features significantly in ''[[The Hobbit]]'' and in the film ''[[The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug]]''.

The term ''Mirkwood'' derives from the forest ''[[Myrkviðr]]'' of [[Norse mythology]]; that forest has been identified by scholars as representing a wooded region of Ukraine at the time of the wars between the [[Goths]] and the [[Huns]] in the fourth century. A Mirkwood was used by Scott in his 1814 novel ''[[Waverley (novel)|Waverley]]'', and then by Morris in his 1889 fantasy novel ''[[The House of the Wolfings]]''. [[Forest]]s play a major role in the invented history of Tolkien's Middle-earth and are important in the heroic quests of his characters.<ref name="NYT 1938">Eaton, Anne T. ''[[The New York Times]]'' Book Review, ''[[The Hobbit]]'', March 13, 1938, "After the dwarves and Bilbo have passed ...over the Misty Mountains and through ''forests that suggest those of William Morris's prose romances''." (emphasis added)</ref> The forest device is used as a mysterious transition from one part of the story to another.<ref>[[Jared Lobdell|Lobdell, Jared]] [1975]. ''[[A Tolkien Compass]]''. La Salle, Illinois: Open Court. {{ISBN|0-87548-316-X}}. p. 84, "only look at ''The Lord of the Rings'' for the briefest of times to catch a vision of ancient forests, of trees like men walking, of leaves and sunlight, and of deep shadows."</ref>

== In Walter Scott's ''Waverley'' ==

A forest called Mirkwood was used by [[Walter Scott]] in his 1814 novel ''[[Waverley (novel)|Waverley]]'', which had

{{blockquote|a rude and contracted path through the cliffy and woody pass called Mirkwood Dingle, and opened suddenly upon a deep, dark, and small lake, named, from the same cause, Mirkwood-Mere. There stood, in former times, a solitary tower upon a rock almost surrounded by the water ...<ref>{{cite journal |last=Orth |first=John V. |author-link=John V. Orth<!--yes, the lawyer, see https://dc.swosu.edu/mythlore/vol38/iss1/31/--> |title=Mirkwood |journal=Mythlore |date=2019 |volume=38 |issue=1 (Fall/Winter) |pages=51–53 |url=https://dc.swosu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2481&context=mythlore}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Scott |first=Walter |author-link=Walter Scott |title=Waverley; or, 'Tis Sixty Years Since. In Three Volumes |date=1814 |publisher=[[Archibald Constable]]}}</ref>}}

== In William Morris's fantasies ==

[[William Morris]] used Mirkwood in his fantasy novels. His 1889 ''[[The Roots of the Mountains]]'' is set in such a forest,<ref name="Drout2007"/> while the forest setting in his ''[[The House of the Wolfings]]'', also first published in 1889, is actually named ''Mirkwood''. The book begins by describing the wood:

{{blockquote|The tale tells that in times long past there was a dwelling of men beside a great wood. Before it lay a plain, not very great, but which was, as it were, an isle in the sea of woodland, since even when you stood on the flat ground, you could see trees everywhere in the offing, though as for hills, you could scarce say that there were any; only swellings-up of the earth here and there, like the upheavings of the water that one sees at whiles going on amidst the eddies of a swift but deep stream.

On either side, to right and left the tree-girdle reached out toward the blue distance, thick close and unsundered ...

In such wise that Folk had made an island amidst of the Mirkwood, and established a home there, and upheld it with manifold toil too long to tell of. And from the beginning this clearing in the wood they called the Mid-mark ...<ref name="Morris Wolfings 1889">{{cite book |last=Morris |first=William |author-link=William Morris |title=The House of the Wolfings |publisher=Longmans, Green, and Co. |year=1904 |orig-year=1889 |page=start of chapter 1 |url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/2885/2885-h/2885-h.htm}}</ref>}}

== In Tolkien's writings ==

{{further|Forests in Middle-earth|Tolkien and the Norse}}

A Mirkwood appears in several places in [[J. R. R. Tolkien]]'s writings, among the numerous forests that play important roles in his storytelling.<ref name="NYT 1938"/> Projected into [[Old English language|Old English]], it appears as ''Myrcwudu'' in his ''[[The Lost Road and Other Writings|The Lost Road]]'', as a poem sung by [[Ælfwine of England|Ælfwine]].<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1987}}, ''[[King Sheave]]'', 91</ref> He used the name Mirkwood in another unfinished work, ''[[The Fall of Arthur]]''.<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|2013}}, pp. 19 & 22</ref> But the name is best known and most prominent in his [[Middle-earth]] legendarium, where it appears as two distinct forests, one in the [[First Age]] in [[Beleriand]], as described in ''[[The Silmarillion]]'', the other in the [[Third Age]] in Rhovanion, as described in both ''[[The Hobbit]]'' and ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]''.<ref name="Drout2007"/>

Tolkien stated in a 1966 letter that he had not invented the name Mirkwood, but that it was "a very ancient name, weighted with legendary associations", and summarized its "Primitive Germanic" origins, its appearance in "very early German" and in Old English, [[Old Swedish]], and [[Old Norse]], and the survival of [[wikt:mirk|mirk]] (a variant of "murk") in modern English. He wrote that "It seemed to me too good a fortune that Mirkwood remained intelligible (with exactly the right tone) in modern English to pass over: whether mirk is a Norse loan or a freshment of the obsolescent O.E. word."<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Carpenter|2023|loc=#289 to Michael George Tolkien, 29 July 1966 }}</ref> He was familiar with Morris's ''The House of the Wolfings'', naming the book as an influence (for instance on the [[Dead Marshes]]) in a 1960 letter.<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Carpenter|2023|loc=#226 to Professor L. W. Forster, 31 December 1960 }}</ref>

=== The First Age forest in Beleriand ===

{{further|Beleriand}}

In ''The Silmarillion'', the forested highlands of Dorthonion in the north of Beleriand (in the northwest of Middle-earth) eventually fell under [[Morgoth]]'s control and was subjugated by creatures of [[Sauron]], then Lord of Werewolves. Accordingly, the forest was renamed ''Taur-nu-Fuin'' in [[Sindarin]], "Forest of Darkness", or "Forest of Nightshade";<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1977}}, "Quenta Silmarillion: Of the Ruin of Beleriand and the Fall of Fingolfin"</ref> Tolkien chose to use the English form "Mirkwood". [[Beren]] becomes the sole survivor of the men who once lived there as subjects of the [[Noldor]] King [[Finrod]] of [[Nargothrond]]. Beren ultimately escapes the terrible forest that even the [[Orc]]s fear to spend time in.<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1985}}, p. 36, "but dread they know of the Deadly Nightshade and in haste only do they hie that way."</ref> [[Beleg]] pursues the captors of [[Túrin]] through this forest in the several accounts of Túrin's tale. Along with the rest of Beleriand, this forest was lost in the cataclysm of the [[War of Wrath]] at the end of the First Age.<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1977}}, Index entry "Beleriand": "Beleriand was broken in the turmoils at the end of the First Age, and invaded by the sea, so that only Ossiriand (Lindon) remained." See pages 120-124, 252, 285-286</ref>

{{anchor|Rhovanion}}

=== The forest in Rhovanion ===

{{further|William Morris's influence on Tolkien}}

{{Sketch Map of Middle-earth|upright=1.8|position=right|caption=Imagemap with clickable links of the north-west of [[Middle-earth]] at the end of the [[Third Age]]. Mirkwood is to the east of the Misty Mountains.}}

Mirkwood is a vast [[temperate broadleaf and mixed forest]] in the [[Middle-earth]] region of Rhovanion (Wilderland), east of the great river [[Geography of Middle-earth#Rhovanion|Anduin]]. In ''The Hobbit'', the wizard [[Gandalf]] calls it "the greatest forest of the Northern world."<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1937}}, ch. 7 "Queer Lodgings"</ref> Before it was darkened by evil, it had been called Greenwood the Great.<ref name="Of the Rings of Power" group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1977}}, "Of the Rings of Power and the Third Age"</ref> Tolkien [[Tolkien's maps#The Hobbit|charted]] Mirkwood in ''Thror's Map'' and the ''Map of Wilderland'', which formed endleaves to ''The Hobbit''. Within the text, an ink illustration captioned 'The Elvenking's Gate' depicts the entrance to King [[Thranduil]]'s kingdom.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hammond |first=Wayne G. |title=The art of the Hobbit by J.R.R. Tolkien |last2=Tolkien |first2=J. R. R. |last3=Scull |first3=Christina |date=2011 |publisher=HarperCollins |isbn=978-0-00-744081-8 |location=London |pages=12-15}}</ref>

After the publication of [[Tolkien's maps|the maps]] in ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]'', Tolkien wrote a correction stating "Mirkwood is too small on map it must be 300 miles across" from east to west,<ref>{{cite book |last=Rateliff |first=John D. |author-link=John D. Rateliff |title=[[The History of The Hobbit]] |year=2007 |publisher=HarperCollins |chapter=Part 2, The Fifth Phase, Timelines and Itinerary (ii) |page=821 |isbn=978-0-00-725066-0}}</ref> but the maps were never altered to reflect this. On the published maps, Mirkwood was up to {{convert|200|mi|km}} across; from north to south it stretched about {{convert|420|mi|km}}.<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954a}} and {{harvnb|Tolkien|1954}}, fold-out maps</ref> The ''[[J. R. R. Tolkien Encyclopedia]]'' states that it is {{convert|400|–|500|mi|km}} long and {{convert|200|mi|km}} wide.<ref name="Drout2007">{{cite book |chapter=Mirkwood |last=Evans |first=Jonathan |author-link=Jonathan Evans (scholar) |title=J. R. R. Tolkien Encyclopedia: Scholarship and Critical Assessment |title-link=J. R. R. Tolkien Encyclopedia |editor=Drout, Michael D. C. |editor-link=Michael D. C. Drout |publisher=[[Routledge]]|year=2006 |pages=429–430 |isbn=0-415-96942-5}}</ref>

The trees were large and densely packed. In the north they were mainly [[Quercus robur|oak]]s, although [[Fagus sylvatica|beeches]] predominated in the areas favoured by [[Silvan Elves|Elves]].<ref name="Drout2007"/> Higher elevations in southern Mirkwood were "clad in a forest of dark [[fir]]".<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954a}}, book 2 ch. 6 "Lothlórien"</ref><ref name="Drout2007"/> Pockets of the forest were dominated by dangerous giant spiders.<ref name="TTT book 4 ch 9" group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954}}, book 4, ch. 9 "Shelob's Lair"</ref> Animals within the forest were described as inedible.<ref name="Flies and Spiders" group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1937}}, ch. 8, "Flies and Spiders"</ref> The elves of the forest, too, are "black" and hostile, drawing a comparison with ''Svartalfheim'' ("Black elf home") in [[Snorri Sturluson]]'s Old Norse ''Edda'', quite unlike the friendly elves of [[Rivendell]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Rings, dwarves, elves and dragons: J. R. R. Tolkien's Old Norse influences |url=https://www.uhi.ac.uk/en/research-enterprise/cultural/institute-for-northern-studies/social-media--blogs/mimirs-well-articles/rings-dwarves-elves-and-dragons-j-r-r-tolkiens-old-norse-influences.html# |publisher=Institute for Northern Studies, [[University of the Highlands and Islands]] [of Scotland] |date=9 October 2017 |access-date=22 May 2020}}</ref>

Near the end of the [[Third Age]] – the period in which ''The Hobbit'' and ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]'' are set – the expansive forest of "Greenwood the Great" was renamed "Mirkwood", [[Pseudotranslation in The Lord of the Rings|supposedly a translation]] of an unknown [[Westron]] name.<ref name=Foster1971>{{cite book |last=Foster |first=Robert |author-link=Robert Foster (author) |title=A Guide to Middle Earth |publisher=[[Ballantine Books]] |year=1971 |pages=174, 251}}</ref> The forest plays little part in ''The Lord of the Rings'', but is important in ''The Hobbit'' for both atmosphere and plot.<ref name="Drout2007"/> It was renamed when "the shadow of [[Dol Guldur]]", namely the power of [[Sauron]], fell upon the forest, and people began to call it ''Taur-nu-Fuin'' ([[Sindarin]]: "forest under deadly nightshade" or "forest under night", i.e. "mirk wood") and ''Taur-e-Ndaedelos'' (Sindarin: "forest of great fear").<ref name="Drout2007"/><ref name=Foster1971/>

In ''[[The Hobbit]]'', [[Bilbo Baggins]], with [[Thorin Oakenshield]] and his [[List of The Hobbit characters#Thorin's company|band of Dwarves]], attempt to cross Mirkwood during their quest to regain their mountain [[Erebor]] and its treasure from [[Smaug]] the [[Dragon (Middle-earth)|dragon]]. One of the Dwarves, the fat Bombur, falls into the Enchanted River and has to be carried, unconscious, for the following days. Losing the Elf-path, the party becomes lost in the forest and is captured by giant spiders.<ref name="Flies and Spiders" group=T/> They escape, only to be taken prisoner by King Thranduil's Wood-Elves.<ref name="Barrels out of Bond" group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1937}}, ch. 9 "Barrels Out of Bond"</ref> The [[White Council]] flushes Sauron out of his forest tower at Dol Guldur, and as he flees to [[Mordor]] his influence in Mirkwood diminishes.<ref name="Council of Elrond" group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1954a}}, book 2, ch. 2 "[[The Council of Elrond]]"</ref>

Years later, [[Gollum]], after his release from Mordor, is captured by [[Aragorn]] and brought as a prisoner to Thranduil's realm. Out of pity, they allow him to roam the forest under close guard, but he escapes during an [[Orc (Middle-earth)|Orc]] raid. After the downfall of Sauron, Mirkwood is cleansed by the elf-queen [[Galadriel]] and renamed ''Eryn Lasgalen'', [[Sindarin]] for "Wood of Greenleaves". Thranduil's son, [[Legolas]], leaves Mirkwood for [[Ithilien]].<ref group=T>{{harvnb|Tolkien|1955}} book 6 ch. 4, and Appendix B "Later Events"</ref> The [[Wizard (Middle-earth)|wizard]] [[Radagast]] lived at Rhosgobel on the western eaves of Mirkwood,<ref>{{cite journal |last=Birns |first=Nicholas |author-link=Nicholas Birns |title=The Enigma of Radagast: Revision, Melodrama, and Depth |journal=[[Mythlore]] |date=15 October 2007 |volume=26 |issue=1 |at=Article 1 |url=https://dc.swosu.edu/mythlore/vol26/iss1/8}}</ref> as depicted in the film ''[[The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Loinaz |first1=Alexis L. |title=The Hobbit: A Who's-Who Guide to Kick Off An Unexpected Journey |url=https://www.eonline.com/uk/news/370983/the-hobbit-a-who-s-who-guide-to-kick-off-an-unexpected-journey |website=Enews |access-date=22 May 2020 |date=14 December 2012}}</ref>

==== Dol Guldur ====

 	
'''Dol<!--redirects here--> Guldur''' ([[Sindarin]]: "Hill of Sorcery")<ref group=T>''[[The Silmarillion]]'', Index, p. 324.</ref> was Sauron's stronghold in Mirkwood, before he returned to [[Barad-dûr]] in [[Mordor]]. It is first mentioned (as "the dungeons of the Necromancer") in ''[[The Hobbit]]''.<ref group=T>''[[The Hobbit]]'', "An Unexpected Party", p. 34.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Nelson |first=Charles W. |title=J.R.R. Tolkien and His Literary Resonances: Views of Middle-earth |publisher=Greenwood Press |year=2000 |page=86 |chapter=6: The sins of Middle-earth, Tolkien's use of Allegory}}</ref> The hill itself, rocky and barren, was the highest point in the southwestern part of the forest. Before Sauron's occupation, it was called Amon Lanc ("Naked Hill"<ref group=T>''[[Unfinished Tales]]'', Index, p. 418.</ref>).<ref group=T>''[[Unfinished Tales]]'', "Disaster of the Gladden Fields", p. 280, note 12.</ref> It lay near the western edge of the forest, across the [[Geography of Middle-earth#Rhovanion|Anduin]] from [[Lothlórien]].<ref group=T>''[[The Fellowship of the Ring]]'', "Lothlórien", p. 366.</ref> Tolkien suggests that Sauron settled on Dol Guldur as the focus for his rise during the period before the [[War of the Ring]] in part so that he could search for the [[One Ring]] in the [[Gladden Fields]] just up the river.<ref group=T>See for example, ''[[The Silmarillion]]'', "Of the Rings of Power and the Third Age", p. 302.</ref>

== Literary philology ==

{{further|Myrkviðr|Hlöðskviða}}

[[File:Mirkwood between the Carpathians and Dnieper.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|Possible location of Mirkwood in the 4th-century [[Goths|Goth]]–[[Huns|Hun]] borderlands between the [[Carpathian Mountains]] and the [[River Dnieper]], both mentioned in Norse legend.<ref name="Shippey 2007"/> The arrows indicate the movement of the peoples after meeting.]]

19th-century writers interested in philology, including the folklorist [[Jacob Grimm]] and the artist and fantasy writer [[William Morris]], speculated romantically about the wild, primitive Northern forest, the ''Myrkviðr inn ókunni'' ("the pathless Mirkwood") and the secret roads across it, in the hope of reconstructing supposed ancient cultures.<ref name="Drout2007"/><ref name="Shippey2014"/> Grimm proposed that the name ''Myrkviðr'' derived from Old Norse ''mark'' (boundary) and ''mǫrk'' (forest), both, he supposed, from an older word for wood, perhaps at the dangerous and disputed boundary of the kingdoms of the [[Huns]] and the [[Goths]].<ref name="Drout2007"/><ref name="Shippey 1982">[[Tom Shippey|Shippey, Tom]]. "Goths and Huns: the rediscovery of the Northern cultures in the nineteenth century". in ''The Medieval Legacy: A Symposium.'' ed. Andreas Haarder et al. Odense University Press, 1982. pp. 51–69.</ref>

Morris's Mirkwood is named in his 1899 fantasy novel ''House of the Wolfings'',<ref name="Morris Wolfings 1889"/> and a similar large dark forest is the setting in ''The Roots of the Mountains'', again marking a dark and dangerous forest.<ref name="Drout2007"/> Tolkien had access to more modern [[philology]] than Grimm, with [[proto-Indo-European]] ''mer-'' (to flicker [dimly]) and ''*merg-'' (mark, boundary), and places the early origins of both the Men of Rohan and the hobbits in his Mirkwood.<ref name="Drout2007"/> The ''Tolkien Encyclopedia'' remarks also that the [[Old English]] ''[[Beowulf]]'' mentions that the path between the worlds of men and monsters, from [[Hrothgar]]'s hall to [[Grendel]]'s lair, runs ''ofer myrcan mor'' (across a gloomy moor) and ''wynleasne wudu'' (a joyless wood).<ref name="Drout2007"/>

A Mirkwood is mentioned in multiple Norse texts including ''[[Sögubrot af nokkrum fornkonungum]]'', ''[[Helgakviða Hundingsbana I and II]]'', ''[[Styrbjarnar þáttr Svíakappa]]'', and ''[[Völundarkviða]]''; these mentions may have denoted different forests.<ref name="Kenyon 2020">{{cite web |last=Kenyon |first=Matthew |title=The Fall of the Burgundians: Continuity in Legend and History |url=https://skemman.is/bitstream/1946/35428/1/Fall%20of%20the%20Burgundians.pdf |publisher=University of Iceland (MA Thesis) |access-date=9 March 2021 |page=28 |date=May 2020}}</ref> The Goths had lived in Ukraine until the attack by the Huns in the 370s, when they moved southwest and with the permission of the Emperor [[Valens]] settled in the Roman Empire.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kulikowski |first=Michael |author-link=Michael Kulikowski |year=2006 |title=Rome's Gothic Wars: From the Third Century to Alaric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QXM9SH4EALgC |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |isbn=978-1139458092 |page=130}}</ref> The scholar [[Omeljan Pritsak]] identifies the Mirkwood of ''Hlöðskviða'' in ''Hervarar saga'' with what would later be called the "dark blue forest" (''Goluboj lěsь'') and the  "black forest" (''Černyj lěsь'') north of the Ukrainian steppe.<ref name="Pritsak">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Eggers |first=M. |volume=20 |article=Myrkviðr |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CvSk4Ds393oC&pg=PA460 |title=Reallexikon der germansichen Altertumskunde |trans-title=Dictionary of Germanic Antiquity |edition=2 |editor-last1=Beck |editor-first1=Heinrich |year=2002 |pages=460–461|publisher=Walter de Gruyter |isbn=9783110171648 }}</ref>

[[Tom Shippey]] noted that Norse legend yields two placenames which would place the ''Myrkviðr'' in the borderlands between the Goths and the Huns of the 4th century. The ''[[Atlakviða]]'' ("The Lay of Atli", in the [[Elder Edda]]) and the ''[[Hlöðskviða]]'' ("The Battle of the Goths and Huns", in ''[[Hervarar saga ok Heiðreks]]'') both mention that the Mirkwood was beside the ''Danpar'', the [[River Dnieper]], which runs through [[Ukraine]] to the [[Black Sea]]. The ''Hlöðskviða'' states explicitly in the same passage that the Mirkwood was in Gothland. The ''Hervarar saga'' also mentions ''Harvaða fjöllum'', "the Harvad fells", which by [[Grimm's Law]] would be ''*Karpat'', the [[Carpathian Mountains]],<ref name="Shippey 2007">{{cite book |last=Shippey |first=Tom |author-link=Tom Shippey |chapter=Goths and Huns: The Rediscovery of the Northern Cultures in the Nineteenth Century |title=Roots and Branches |date=2007 |publisher=Walking Tree Publishers |isbn=978-3905703054 |pages=115–136}}</ref><ref name="carpathians.pl">[http://www.carpathians.pl/carpathians01.html About the Carpathians - Carpathian Heritage Society] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100406010559/http://www.carpathians.pl/carpathians01.html |date=6 April 2010}}</ref> an identification on which most scholars have long agreed.<ref>Pritsak, Omeljan (1981). The origin of Rus'. Harvard University Press. p.199</ref>

== Influence ==

=== Mirkwood ===

Tolkien's estate disputed the right of the [[Tolkien fan fiction]] author [[Steve Hillard]] "to use the name and personality of J. R. R. Tolkien in the novel" ''Mirkwood: A Novel About J. R. R. Tolkien''.<ref name="Alberge 2011">{{cite news |last=Alberge |first=Dalya |title=JRR Tolkien novel Mirkwood in legal battle with author's estate |url=https://www.theguardian.com/books/2011/feb/26/mirkwood-jrr-tolkien-legal-battle |work=[[The Guardian]] |date=26 February 2011}}</ref> The dispute was settled in May 2011, requiring the printing of a disclaimer.<ref>{{cite web |last=Gardner |first=Eriq |title=JRR Tolkien Estate Settles Dispute Over Novel Featuring Tolkien As Character |date=2 May 2011 |work=The Hollywood Reporter |url=http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/thr-esq/jrr-tolkien-estate-settles-dispute-184053}}</ref>
A rock music group named [[Mirkwood (band)|Mirkwood]] was formed in 1971; their first album in 1973 had the same name. A different band in California used the name in 2005.<ref>{{cite web |title=Mirkwood (2) |url=https://www.discogs.com/artist/2048529-Mirkwood-2 |website=Discogs |access-date=7 August 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Mirkwood |url=https://mirkwoodband.bandcamp.com/ |website=Bandcamp |access-date=7 August 2025 |language=en}}</ref>

Tolkien's forests were the subject of a programme on [[BBC Radio 3]], with [[Eleanor Rosamund Barraclough]] and the folk singer Mark Atherton.<ref>{{cite web |title=BBC Radio Programme on Tolkien's Forest: Mirkwood |url=https://www.tolkiensociety.org/2018/10/bbc-radio-programme-on-tolkiens-forest-mirkwood/ |publisher=Tolkien Society |date=16 October 2018 |access-date=22 May 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Barraclough |first=Eleanor Rosamund |title=Mirkwood {{!}} Forests |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m0000qj9 |publisher=[[BBC Radio 3]] |date=9 September 2019 |access-date=22 May 2020}} Available at [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cr0VE31npaA The Supernatural North, a documentary, 2017]</ref>
Literary holidays in the [[Forest of Dean]] have been sold on the basis that the area inspired Tolkien, who often went there, to create Mirkwood and [[Forests in Middle-earth|other forests in his books]].<ref>{{cite web |title='H' is for Hobbit… |url=https://www.classicbritishhotels.com/12-literary-landscapes-bard-beatrix-miss-moneypenny-middle-earth/ |publisher=Classic British Hotels |access-date=8 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161215115358/https://www.classicbritishhotels.com/12-literary-landscapes-bard-beatrix-miss-moneypenny-middle-earth/ |archive-date=15 December 2016 |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Dol Guldur ===


Dol Guldur has been featured in many game adaptations of ''[[The Lord of the Rings]]'', including the [[Iron Crown Enterprises]] portrayal, which contains scenarios and adventures for the [[Middle-earth Role Playing]] game.<ref>[http://www.icewebring.com/ICE_Products/M2/M2_2014_Dol_Guldur.php MERP 2014 Dol Guldur] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071114171453/http://www.icewebring.com/ICE_Products/M2/M2_2014_Dol_Guldur.php |date=14 November 2007 }}</ref> In the strategy battle game ''[[The Lord of the Rings: The Battle for Middle-earth II]]'', Dol Guldur appears as an iconic building.<ref>McGregor, Georgia Leigh. ''Architecture, space and gameplay in World of Warcraft and Battle for Middle Earth 2'', ACM International Conference Proceeding Series; Vol. 223, Murdoch University, 2006 {{ISBN|0-86905-901-7}}</ref><ref name="Architecture, Space and Gameplay in BFME2 and WOW">{{cite web |url=http://www.users.on.net/~georgia88/files/Architecture,%20Space%20and%20Gameplay%20-%20Georgia%20Leigh%20McGregor.pdf |title=Architecture, Space and Gameplay in BFME2 and WOW |publisher=University of New South Wales |access-date=21 August 2008 |archive-date=11 February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080211222335/http://www.users.on.net/~georgia88/files/Architecture,%20Space%20and%20Gameplay%20-%20Georgia%20Leigh%20McGregor.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The campaign-scenario called "Assault on Dol Guldur" appears as the final part of the good campaign.<ref name="Official Game">''The Lord of the Rings: Battle for Middle-earth II''. EA Games, 2006. See detailed map. EAN 5030930050368.</ref><ref name="xbox360achievements">{{cite web |url=http://www.xbox360achievements.org/guide.php?type=Retail&gameID=74 |title=Achievement Guide  |work=xbox360achievements.com |pages=1 |access-date=2008-06-01 |archive-date=2011-10-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001035439/http://www.xbox360achievements.org/guide.php?type=Retail&gameID=74 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Several portrayals of Dol Guldur are included in the [[Games Workshop]] game ''[[The Lord of the Rings Strategy Battle Game]]'', appearing prominently in the "Fall of the Necromancer". Several enemies are listed, including Spider Queens,<ref name="Games Workshop">{{cite web |url=http://uk.games-workshop.com/dolguldur/spider-conversions/1/ |title=Scourges of Mirkwood: Converting unique Spider Queens |publisher=Games Workshop Online |access-date=31 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080512035815/http://uk.games-workshop.com/dolguldur/spider-conversions/1/ |archive-date=12 May 2008}}</ref> Castellans of Dol Guldur, Sauron the Necromancer, Wild [[Warg (Middle-earth)|Warg]] Chieftain, and their respective armies. Giant Bats are also included in the game.<ref name="Games Workshop Online 2">{{cite web|url=http://uk.games-workshop.com/dolguldur/miniature-gallery/1/|title=Denizens of Dol Guldur: Dol Guldur Miniatures Gallery |author=Games Workshop Online |publisher=Games Workshop Online |access-date=31 May 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080706191816/http://uk.games-workshop.com/dolguldur/miniature-gallery/1/ |archive-date=6 July 2008}}</ref> In 1996, the black metal band [[Summoning (band)|Summoning]] released a music album named ''[[Dol Guldur (album)|Dol Guldur]]''.<ref name="Album">{{cite AV media |title=Dol Guldur |author=[[Summoning (band)|Summoning]] |publisher=[[Napalm Records]] |date=2007 |url=https://www.amazon.com/Dol-Guldur-Summoning/dp/B000GEU6JU |access-date=1 June 2008}}</ref>

The Canadian artist [[John Howe (illustrator)|John Howe]] has portrayed Dol Guldur in sketches and drawings for [[Electronic Arts]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Howe |first=John |author-link=John Howe (illustrator) |url=http://www.john-howe.com/portfolio/gallery/search.php?sessionid=4f50f48f65c3d9513712a1a2be677280 |title=John Howe Dol Guldur portfolio |publisher=John Howe |access-date=19 June 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.john-howe.com/portfolio/gallery/details.php?image_id=3549&mode=search |title=Electronic Arts design |publisher=John Howe |access-date=19 June 2008}}</ref> In ''Myth and Magic: The Art of John Howe'', Howe includes Dol Guldur among Middle-earth fortresses.<ref name="Myth&Magic">{{cite book |last=Howe |first=John |author-link=John Howe (illustrator) |last2=Jackson |first2=Peter |author-link2=Peter Jackson |last3=Lee |first3=Alan |author-link3=Alan Lee (illustrator) |last4=McKellen |first4=Ian |author-link4=Ian McKellen |last5=Holdstock |first5=Robin |author-link5=Robert Holdstock |last6=Hobb |first6=Robin |author-link6=Robin Hobb |title=Myth and Magic: The Art of John Howe |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |date=3 December 2001 |pages=144 |isbn=0-00-710795-1 |url=http://www.john-howe.com/portfolio/gallery/details.php?image_id=1543&mode=search}}</ref> Howe created many drawings for [[Peter Jackson]] during the filming of the [[The Lord of the Rings (film series)|''Lord of the Rings'' trilogy]], worked for Tolkien Enterprises, and drew for Iron Crown Enterprises' collectable Middle-earth card game, which mentions Dol Guldur on Gandalf's card.<ref>{{cite web |last=Howe |first=John |author-link=John Howe (illustrator) |url=http://www.john-howe.com/portfolio/gallery/details.php?image_id=198&mode=search |title=Middle-earth collectable card game |publisher=John Howe |access-date=19 June 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Howe |first=John |author-link=John Howe (illustrator) |url=http://www.john-howe.com/portfolio/gallery/details.php?image_id=327&mode=search |title=Gandalf |publisher=John Howe |access-date=19 June 2008}}</ref> Mirkwood was added to the [[massively multiplayer online role-playing game|MMORPG]] ''[[The Lord of the Rings Online: Shadows of Angmar]]'' in the 2009 expansion pack ''Siege of Mirkwood''. The storyline depicts a small Elven assault upon Dol Guldur.

In [[Peter Jackson]]'s 2012–2014 [[The Hobbit film series|film trilogy adaptation]] of ''[[The Hobbit]]'', Dol Guldur is depicted as a massive overgrown castle in ruins. According to [[Alan Lee (illustrator)|Alan Lee]] and John Howe, the [[concept artist]]s, this was used to give the impression that the fortress had been built by [[Númenór]]eans during the Second Age, only to fall into ruin when Númenór's power waned.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sibley |first=Brian |author-link=Brian Sibley |title=The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug Official Movie Guide |pages=72–78 |date=2013 |publisher=[[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt]] |location=New York}}</ref> Adrián Maldonado of AlmostArchaeology speculates that the derelict castle could be interpreted by viewers as the ruins of Oropher's halls, erected during the Second Age when he ruled Greenwood the Great from Amon Lanc.<ref>{{cite web |last=Maldonado |first=Adrián |title=A Handy Guide to the Archaeology of ''The Hobbit: The Battle of the Five Armies'' |url=https://almostarchaeology.com/post/107749227588/a-handy-guide-to-the-archaeology-of-the-hobbit |publisher=AlmostArchaeology |access-date=18 December 2019 |date=11 January 2015}}</ref>
